issues.explanation: The profile is anchored to physical abuse by a romantic partner, but 'dark spaces' as a trigger and generalized threat from strangers are not well integrated with the rest of the selected items, which otherwise focus on the perpetrator and interpersonal/tactile reminders. This combination is possible, but without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking darkness to the abuse, darkness stands out as a poorly grounded trigger.

issues.item: Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: Feeling threatened by strangers in ordinary situations suggests broad generalized threat, but the rest of the profile does not provide corresponding appraisals or memory content to explain that generalization. The active formulation emphasizes Threat → Maladaptive Strategies, yet the selected strategies are mostly perpetrator- and social-contact-focused rather than stranger-focused, leaving this threat item insufficiently supported.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is an unusual target for avoidance in a case otherwise centered on partner abuse, tactile triggers, similar cars, and perpetrator reminders. It is not directly contradictory, but it does not cohere well with the other items or the active edge structure, because the threat content does not specifically concern familiar social contacts from before the event.

'Car Similarity' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is some clear motor-vehicle-specific trauma context, which is not otherwise represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The threat items are dominated by high immediate danger/re-experiencing states (flashbacks, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance), but the formulation has no active Triggers → Threat link and no Memory involvement; this makes a strong trigger-driven reliving/threat profile clinically incoherent with the specified network structure.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Avoidance of perpetrator reminders implies salient perpetrator-linked cueing, but the trigger set mixes direct offender cues with an idiosyncratic 'similar cars' cue that is not supported by the trauma type or by any memory/appraisal content explaining why vehicle similarity would be central.

vignette:
Richard Hale is a 74-year-old widowed American man who spent most of his adult life as a combat pilot, a role that shaped his posture, routines, and sense that he should remain controlled under pressure. He came to treatment only after years of keeping his private life sealed off, and even in the first sessions he spoke carefully, with the restraint of someone used to containing whatever rises inside him. The event he returns to happened late in his marriage, after his wife had been drinking. He described an evening at home when the smell of alcohol met him at the door before he saw her. What followed was not a single blow out of nowhere but a scene he now remembers in sharply physical fragments: her coming toward him unsteadily, the sudden grab at his arm, hands on his chest and shoulders, the force of being shoved and struck in close quarters by someone whose touch should have signaled safety. What remains most vivid to him is the collision of intimacy and danger. He can still picture her face at close range and remember the smell of liquor on her breath as she put her hands on him.

In the period afterward, Richard did not talk about the assault as something that had happened to him. He carried on as if composure itself could settle it. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger about what had happened. In his mind, anger was something dangerous, something that had to be locked down immediately. When flashes of it came up, he pushed them away and straightened himself, as if discipline alone could restore order. What he did notice was how quickly his body reacted in situations that bore even a slight resemblance to that night. If someone touched him unexpectedly, even in ordinary ways, his body jerked before he could think. His chest tightened, his muscles went hard, and he felt the kind of immediate physical surge he could not explain away. The smell of alcohol in restaurants, elevators, or on another person’s clothes could have the same effect, producing a rush of tension that made him want to leave at once.

Because he had once spent his working life in cockpits where constant scanning was adaptive, Richard found it difficult to recognize how relentless his watchfulness had become in civilian life. He stays on guard in waiting rooms, parking lots, and grocery store aisles, noting who is nearby and where the exits are. What frightened him most at night was the sense that letting down his guard would leave him exposed. He has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he needs to stay alert. He lies in bed listening for movement, rehearsing whether doors are locked, feeling as though full sleep would be a mistake. The result is a thin, fractured kind of rest that leaves him tired but no less watchful the next day.

Avoidance settled into his life gradually. Anything that reminded him of his wife became something to evade. If he thought he might encounter places, objects, or social settings linked to her, he altered plans or stayed home. On one occasion he saw a woman at a distance whose build and gait resembled hers, and the jolt of recognition was so strong that he immediately turned away and left before confirming who it was. Seeing the offender herself remains especially potent; even the possibility of it makes his body brace. He also withdrew from closeness with other people. Since being widowed, he has kept emotional distance even from those who have tried to be kind. He does not date, avoids affectionate gestures, and becomes uncomfortable when others move toward intimacy or sustained emotional contact. To him, closeness now carries too much uncertainty, too much risk of being caught off guard by touch.

His occupational identity still structures his days. Though retired from active flying, he remains connected to aviation circles, and those settings make his symptoms visible. At reunions or museum events, handshakes, congratulatory pats on the shoulder, and the smell of alcohol at receptions can make him suddenly rigid and silent. He positions himself near doors, leaves early, and afterwards tells himself he simply prefers solitude. Over time this has narrowed his world. Friends from his flying years have seen less of him, and family members have learned that he rarely accepts invitations that might involve crowds, drinking, or familiarity.

What finally brought Richard in was not a new event but the accumulation of a life organized around staying braced. He is tired of sleeping lightly, tired of flinching from touch, tired of feeling his body overreact before he has had a chance to think. He is also ashamed of how much he has hidden behind self-control. He said he wants help because he does not want the rest of his life defined by avoidance and vigilance. At the same time, he is afraid that if he loosens his grip even slightly—if he allows anger, closeness, or sleep—he will lose the only protections he feels he has.
